subject: community-medicine
title: Dispersion: Range, Variance, and Standard Deviation

steps.title: Why averages alone mislead
steps.tx: Two villages can share a mean haemoglobin of eleven grams yet differ completely: one clusters tightly, the other splits between severe anaemia and high values. **Measures of dispersion** quantify that scatter around the average. Without them, means conceal inequality, laboratory imprecision, and outbreak heterogeneity, which is why every thesis table pairs each mean with a standard deviation or median with an interquartile range.
steps.say: Same mean, different scatter, different story. Always report spread beside the average.

steps.title: Range: the crudest spread
steps.tx: The **range in descriptive statistics** is simply the maximum minus the minimum (or the interval between them). It needs two seconds to compute, serves quality control charts and weather reports, but depends on exactly two extreme values, grows with sample size, and ignores the interior entirely. One data entry error can double it, so it never stands alone in serious reporting.
steps.say: Range is maximum minus minimum: quick but fragile. One typo can double it.

steps.title: Mean deviation
steps.tx: Averaging the absolute departures from the mean gives the **mean deviation** (average deviation), an intuitive spread in original units that uses every observation. It lost favour historically because absolute values resist algebra, but its robust descendant, the median absolute deviation, now serves outlier detection in laboratory and survey data where standard deviations would be corrupted by the very extremes under hunt.
steps.say: Mean deviation averages distances from the mean in plain units. Its median based cousin hunts outliers today.

steps.title: Variance: squared departures
steps.tx: Squaring departures before averaging yields the **variance**, which punishes distant values quadratically and unlocks beautiful algebra: variances of independent variables add. Population variance divides by N; sample variance divides by n minus one (Bessel correction) because the sample mean itself consumes one degree of freedom and otherwise underestimates spread. Squared units (centimetres squared) are the price paid.
steps.say: Variance averages squared distances and divides samples by n minus one. Its units are squared, so we take the root next.

steps.title: Standard deviation: the working measure
steps.tx: The square root of variance is the **standard deviation**, restoring original units and becoming the universal partner of the mean. It measures typical distance from the mean, defines normal distribution bands, and feeds standard errors, z scores, and t tests. In a normal distribution about sixty eight percent of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean, the bridge to the next lessons.
steps.say: Standard deviation is the root of variance, back in real units. It is the spread measure every later test consumes.

steps.tx: Shaded bands on a normal curve mark where values cluster around the mean. The **standard deviation** is the square root of variance, which returns the original units and describes a typical distance from that mean. About 68 percent of observations fall in the central band, near 95 percent within two deviations, and near 99.7 percent within three. The same figure also enters z scores and the t test.
steps.say: Shaded bands on a normal curve mark where values cluster around the mean. steps.title: Computing SD from grouped data
steps.tx: For frequency tables the **standard deviation calculation** multiplies squared deviations of class marks from the mean by class frequencies, sums, divides by total frequency (or n minus one for samples), and takes the root. Assumed mean shortcuts shift the origin to simplify arithmetic without changing the result. Examinations still reward knowing denominator choice more than button pressing speed.
steps.say: Group marks, weight by frequency, divide correctly, then root. Samples divide by n minus one.

steps.title: Interquartile range for skewed data
steps.tx: Where the median leads, the **interquartile range** follows: the distance between the third and first quartiles (seventy fifth and twenty fifth percentiles), covering the middle fifty percent of values. It ignores tails completely, survives open ended classes, and pairs with the median in every skewed report (hospital stay, income, incubation period). Box plots draw it literally as the box.
steps.say: Interquartile range spans the middle half of the data. It partners the median wherever data are skewed.

steps.title: Standard deviation versus standard error (preview)
steps.tx: Confusing these two is the commonest viva error: the **standard deviation versus standard error** distinction separates describing data from estimating precision. Standard deviation describes scatter of individuals and stays stable as samples grow; standard error describes scatter of sample means and shrinks with root n. The full standard error treatment arrives with the z score lesson; the seed distinction belongs here.
steps.say: Standard deviation describes people; standard error describes means. One stays, the other shrinks with sample size.

steps.title: Choosing the dispersion measure
steps.tx: Close with the matching discipline for **choosing a measure of dispersion**: range for instant field impressions, interquartile range beside medians, standard deviation beside means, and variance when algebra (pooling, analysis of variance) lies ahead. A stem mentioning skewed data with median answered wants interquartile range; one feeding a t test wants standard deviation. The pair must always match the average chosen.
steps.say: Match spread to average: range for speed, IQR for median, SD for mean. Examiners test the pairing, not the arithmetic.
